title: Credibility Booster: How to Get Better at Authoritative Teacher Presence
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Drawing on his colleague Lynsay Fabio's work, Stuart breaks authoritative teacher presence into three learnable, practicable channels: body, voice, and word choice. Body cues include standing tall with feet hips-width apart, squaring up to whoever you're addressing, staying still, relaxing visible tension points, and holding calm eye contact without intimidation. Voice cues include speaking louder than feels natural, ending sentences with a decisive downward inflection, dropping the habit of tacking 'Okay?' onto instructions, staying emotionally neutral even under provocation, and slowing down with deliberate pauses. Word-choice guidance calls for formality (distinct from coldness) during instruction and concision in directions. Stuart closes by recommending teachers rehearse the skill on memorized material before applying it to real instructions, framing authoritative presence as a habit that eventually requires little conscious thought and pays off well beyond the classroom.
points: Stuart distinguishes authoritative presence from authoritarian control, framing it as a constellation of specific, practicable behaviors rather than a personality trait some teachers simply have.

The body guidance singles out feet position as 'especially important for women because we tend to stand with our feet close together to take up less space' — naming a gendered default worth actively countering.
On voice, dropping the habitual 'Okay?' at the end of instructions is framed as a small tell that undermines the appearance of decisiveness, even when the instruction itself is sound.

The recommended rehearsal method — practicing the skill on memorized material like the pledge of allegiance before using it on live instructions — isolates the delivery mechanics from the content, echoing deliberate-practice principles.
quotes: A major part of such a sense in a teacher's room is teacher credibility — that magic sensation when students in the room believe in their hearts that their teacher is good at their job.
Set your feet hips-width apart. Lynsay says this is especially important for women because "we tend to stand with our feet close together to take up less space.
Be loud. Not obnoxiously so, but, in Lynsay's words, "much louder than most people tend to speak." This projects confidence, and it also ensures that all students can clearly hear you.
Don't end instructions with "Okay?" This makes you sound unsure of the instruction you've just given.

Lynsay recommends first practicing authoritative presence with something you know by heart — e.g., the pledge of allegiance or a memorized poem. This lets you focus on the many components of the skill, not the words that you're saying.

Knowing how to convey an authoritative presence helps in all kinds of life domains, not just the classroom. And, once you develop the habit, it tends to be something you need to think very little about.
